definition: Impenetrable means impossible to pass through, enter, or pierce — and, of writing or ideas, impossible to understand.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word impenetrable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know impenetrable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Behind its moat, the citadel's outer wall proved impenetrable to every battering ram the invaders dragged against it.
Thick is the mildest of the three: a thick crowd or thick fog slows your progress without ever quite stopping it, while impenetrable means the way through simply does not exist.
Dense is stronger than thick but still weaker than impenetrable: a dense stretch of forest makes every step a struggle, yet a determined effort gets through — impenetrable means that effort fails.

Impassable is the traveler's word: a flooded road or a snowed-in pass that cannot be crossed. Impenetrable is wider and stricter — it seals a thing against entry of every kind, and it extends to jargon, codes, and expressions, where impassable never goes.

Airtight means sealed so completely that no air slips in or out — said of jars and cabins and, figuratively, of alibis and arguments. Impenetrable needs no seal at all and blocks everything, not just air: a forest, a fortress wall, or a page of legal boilerplate can be impenetrable.

Inscrutable means impossible to read or interpret — said of faces, motives, and silences. Impenetrable can cover baffling writing too, but it starts physical: the wall or thicket nothing gets through, and only then the prose that keeps every reader outside.

Impenetrable is an absolute — reserve it for barriers that truly admit nothing, and reach for thick or dense while a way through still exists.
It moves freely between the physical and the figurative: an impenetrable vault, an impenetrable contract, an impenetrable expression that gives nothing away.
Test writers lean on the figurative use, so expect it attached to prose and plans as often as to walls.
